newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: U.S. says not upping deportations of Nicaraguans.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says not upping deportations of Nicaraguans.

text.p: U.S. Ambassador to Nicaragua John Maisto on Sunday said his government was not increasing the deportation of Nicaraguans living in the United States.

"I can assure the Nicaraguan people there is no policy of mass deportations of Nicaraguans and the numbers show this. The deportation figures for the last two or three years show no change," Maisto said on the Nicaraguan talk show Esta Semana.
"President (Bill) Clinton has repeated this to (Nicaraguan President) Violeta Chamorro on various occassions," he said.
Maisto acknowledged there was a widespread fear of deportation among Nicaraguans in the United States as democratic changes in their home country make it difficult to claim political persecution.

Thousands of Nicaraguans flooded the United States in the 1980s claiming political refugee status from the left-wing Sandinista government, which governed Nicaragua from 1979 to 1990 with Soviet and Cuban backing.
The U.S. government financed right-wing Contra rebels who fought an eight-year civil war against the Sandinistas and offered easy entry for escaping exiles.
But in 1990, President Violeta Chamorro, at the head of a broad centrist coalition, toppled the Sandinistas at the ballot box, ushering in a return of the free market and democracy to Nicaragua.
In 1992, the U.S. government stopped granting political refugee status to Nicaraguans, requiring Nicaraguans in the United States to legalise their status. Many have not done so and fear deportation.
